archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (defense-first)
archetype.definition: A team whose elite, repeatable defense and positive point differential deserve better than 3-3, held back by an offense that turns the ball over and cannot protect or run.

report.headline: An elite defense stuck at .500 by turnovers, sacks and coin-flip losses.
report.take:
Seattle is still built on what made last year's 14-3 team work: a defense that ranked first in EPA allowed in 2025 and sits second this season at -0.113 a play. It allows the fewest yards in the league, gets home at the second-best pressure rate (31.8%), holds offenses to a 28% third-down rate and almost never gives up the explosive pass. None of that is a soft-schedule mirage. The defense has held up against San Francisco's second-ranked offense and Denver alike, and it matches what this staff did a year ago.

The record is about the other side of the ball. The offense ranks 25th in EPA, and the problem is specific. The line allows pressure at the worst rate in football, the run game is 30th in EPA and last in short-yardage conversion, and the team has still leaned run-heavy (27th in pass rate over expected) when passing has been the more efficient play. Drew Lock has started the last five games after Sam Darnold opened the season, and the giveaways have piled up. There were three turnovers at Washington, four against San Francisco and three in the overtime loss at Denver, with five sacks taken in each of the last two. Twelve giveaways in six games have erased most of what the defense creates.

The point differential tells the real story. Seattle is +26, seventh in points per game differential, 12th in net EPA, and the differential implies four wins rather than three. All three losses came by a field goal or less, and each one featured a turnover pile-up. The one oddity on defense is the red zone. Opponents score touchdowns on 78.6% of trips, 30th in the league, from a unit that otherwise allows almost nothing. That is a small-sample number that should drift back toward the defense's overall quality.

Where this goes depends on whether the offense can stop beating itself. The remaining schedule is gentle, with four 2-4 opponents among the next ten and only one game against a top-five offense. A defense this good gives a turnover-neutral offense a path back into the wild-card mix. Without a fix in protection and ball security, it stays a team that outplays opponents on a per-play basis and still splits games.

strengths.title: A top-two defense, again
strengths.body: Seattle ranks second in EPA allowed and first in yards allowed, and it ranked first in defensive EPA in 2025. The quality is spread across pass and run defense, so it does not depend on one matchup. Two years of this level under the same staff make it the most bankable thing about the team.

strengths.title: Pass rush that ends drives
strengths.body: A 31.8% pressure rate and a 21.5% QB-hit rate, both second in the league, feed a 28% third-down conversion rate allowed. Downfield shots are also shut off, with the second-lowest explosive pass rate allowed. Pressure this consistent travels from week to week.

strengths.title: Hidden yards on special teams
strengths.body: Special teams add 3.91 EPA a game, fourth in the league, which matters for a team whose games keep landing within a field goal. The staff has also gone for it on every fourth-down chance its model flagged. Both edges help a low-scoring team flip close games.

concerns.title: Turnovers are deciding the losses
concerns.body: The offense has 12 giveaways in six games. The three losses featured three, four and three turnovers, which wiped out a defense that won the yardage battle. Some of this is volatility that cools, but with Lock under constant pressure it is not purely luck.

concerns.title: Worst pass protection in football
concerns.body: Seattle allows pressure on 31.1% of dropbacks, 32nd, and the QB-hit rate is also last. Lock took five sacks in each of the last two games. Anthony Bradford's return from IR should help at guard, but this has been a structural problem rather than one bad stretch.

concerns.title: A run-first plan without a run game
concerns.body: Run EPA ranks 30th and short-yardage conversion ranks last, yet the offense still runs more than situations call for. That makes third downs longer and the protection problem worse. Zach Charbonnet's possible return could add talent, but the line in front of the backs is the bigger issue.

trend.note: After the 31-7 rout of Arizona, Seattle has lost three of four, each by a field goal or less. Turnovers and sacks have climbed with Lock at quarterback while the defense held steady.

nextGame.headline: Elite Seattle defense meets unbeaten Kansas City in a near coin flip
nextGame.body:
Kansas City arrives 5-0 with the second-best net EPA in the league and the best rushing offense by EPA and yards per carry. That runs straight into a Seattle run defense ranked second by EPA, so the strength-on-strength fight on the ground will shape the game. Seattle has the edge elsewhere. The Chiefs' pass rush ranks 20th in pressure rate and 27th in sacks, which offers Seattle's beleaguered line its softest test in weeks, and Seattle holds a large special-teams edge. The Book makes Seattle a 2.5-point home favorite with a 42.5 total, which fits a game both defenses should keep low.

Availability tilts toward Seattle's pass rush. Kansas City is without tackle Josh Simmons, Jaylon Moore is questionable after a concussion, and the receiver group is thin with Rashee Rice out and Tyquan Thornton on IR. On Seattle's side, guard Bradford has been designated to return and Charbonnet has a good chance to play. Linebacker Drake Thomas, an 87%-snap starter, is out, which matters against the league's best run game. Tight end Elijah Arroyo is out for significant time, which leaves AJ Barner as the lone tight end option against a defense that funnels targets to the position.

waysToWin.title: Rush beats a patched-up tackle group
waysToWin.body: Seattle's second-ranked pressure rate faces a Kansas City line missing Simmons and possibly Moore. The Chiefs have protected well this season, with the third-best sack rate, but that came with their starters in place. Turning that into a couple of drive-ending sacks is the cleanest path.

waysToWin.title: Throw to Barner and the slot
waysToWin.body: Kansas City's defense sends 32.4% of targets against it to tight ends, well above the league share, and grades 29th in EPA allowed to WR3s. Avoiding Jaxon Smith-Njigba's matchup against a defense ranked first against WR1s and working Barner, Kupp and Shaheed underneath is the logical script. Quick throws would also blunt the pressure problem.

waysToWin.title: Win the hidden-yardage game
waysToWin.body: Seattle's special teams rank fourth in EPA while Kansas City's rank 25th. In a game the Book totals at 42.5, field position and a short field or two can decide it.

waysToLose.title: Another turnover pile-up
waysToLose.body: Kansas City leads the league in turnover differential and has won every one-score game it has played. Three giveaways have cost Seattle three games already. Against an opponent this opportunistic, ball security is the whole game.

waysToLose.title: Red-zone trips that end in field goals
waysToLose.body: The Chiefs allow touchdowns on only a third of red-zone trips, second in the league, while Seattle's short-yardage offense ranks last. Drives that stall inside the 20 against a defense this good turn a winnable game into a field-goal exchange Seattle can lose.

waysToLose.title: Kansas City runs through Thomas's absence
waysToLose.body: The league's top rushing offense by EPA gets Seattle without Drake Thomas. Seattle's defense also allows touchdowns on 78.6% of red-zone trips. If the Chiefs can move the ball on the ground, they control the clock and finish drives.

nextGame.watch: How many times Drew Lock is sacked or turns it over against a Kansas City pass rush ranked 20th in pressure rate. If both numbers stay low, Seattle's defense should do the rest.

restOfSeason.body:
The defense is the sustainable part. It has been top-two for a season and a half under this staff, and the red-zone touchdown rate allowed should come down. Seattle's close-game record should also even out, given a point differential that implies a better record than 3-3. The schedule helps, with home games against Arizona, Dallas, the Giants and the Rams, and a trip to a 2-4 Philadelphia team.

The offense caps the ceiling. Protection and the run game look structural rather than unlucky, so expect efficiency to stay below average even as turnovers likely ease from their current rate. A team that wins with defense, special teams and fewer giveaways projects into the nine-to-eleven-win range and the wild-card race. The division title is a long shot with San Francisco at 6-0.
swingFactors: Bradford and Charbonnet returning to fix the run game
Red-zone defense regressing toward its overall level

confidence.note: Six games, a quarterback change and turnover-driven results make the offense hard to read; the defense has two seasons of support.
